channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: Spending on U.S. data center buildings hits record $85 billion annual pace, up 73% in a year — and Census doesn’t count the servers and racks inside
item.description: Tom’s Hardware: “Private data center construction spending is up over 73%, from $49.05 billion to $84.95 billion, year over year (YoY), according to the Census Bureau’s detailed construction spending tables for August. Spending is at a record annual pace, and growth is the fastest since April 2025’s +88.2%. Data center buildouts are now about 63% of all private office construction.”

item.title: AI data centers are coming for federal land. They’re roiling the Nevada governor’s race
item.description: Associated Press: “… over the summer, [Janelle Sorenson] joined with other residents to successfully oppose plans for one of the giant computing warehouses that have popped up around the country. But their victory was short-lived. The developers withdrew their application and instead sought adjacent land owned by the federal government — and the U.S. Bureau of Land Management signed off.”

item.title: Moms for Liberty unleashes AI watchdog on 13,000 school districts to flag controversial policies before votes
item.description: Fox 10 Phoenix: “Moms for Liberty is deploying artificial intelligence to monitor school board agendas across more than 13,000 school districts nationwide, giving parents advance warning about controversial policies before local officials vote on them, Fox News Digital has learned.” I’m tempted to make an non-AI one which does the same thing so you can get advance notice when Moms for Liberty is about to cut up.

item.title: The US Army’s desert tech test shows long road to AI warfare
item.description: Wall Street Journal: “America’s soldiers are still far from reaping the full benefits of cutting-edge autonomous weapons and AI systems, and haven’t been forced by necessity to quickly modernize as militaries like Ukraine’s have in the heat of conflict, current and former national-security officials said. Transforming a land-based fighting force with a history of slow technological adaptation into a nimble organization that makes the most of new innovations has been difficult.”

item.title: Quartz website mainly produced by one AI-assisted reporter writing 50+ stories per day
item.description: Press Gazette: “Respected business title Quartz is using a single, hugely prolific journalist heavily aided by AI to produce nearly all its daily website reporting. It appears to be part of a strategy favouring newsletter output over website journalism.”

item.title: ChatGPT is adding real cartoonists’ signatures to fake New Yorker cartoons
item.description: NiemanLab: “[Brendan] Loper isn’t the only New Yorker cartoonist whose signature has been reproduced by ChatGPT. In the same online forums are dozens of images with those of other prominent contributors, including Harry Bliss, Emily Flake, Joe Dator, Pat Byrnes, Peter Vey, and Jason Adam Katzenstein. In my own tests, ChatGPT output cartoons with signatures of some of the magazine’s most established cartoonists, past and present, including George Booth, Liza Donnelly, Ellis Rosen, and Saul Steinberg.”

item.title: ‘Artificial’ Took on a Big Tech Giant. Hollywood Wasn’t Ready
item.description: Hollywood Reporter: “Luca Guadagnino and star Andrew Garfield speak frankly about what went into their daring film about Sam Altman and OpenAI, and what led to Neon rescuing it after Amazon decided not to release it: ‘The fight is on to make sure that we are allowed to make things freely.'”

item.title: Someone Vibe Coded a Free Knockoff of Adobe Creative Suite
item.description: Gizmodo: “To get this out of the way, you should probably be more cautious than I’ve been about downloading and using a vibe coded piece of software today. Having said that, holy toledo, someone vibe coded their own entire version of Adobe Suite and dumped it on GitHub as open-source software.”

item.title: Just 5 years in, interactive chatbot platform Character.AI files for bankruptcy
item.description: TechCrunch: “Only five years into its journey, Character.AI, which lets users create AI characters and have conversations with them, has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, following a slew of lawsuits and struggles to scale its popular platform. In a court document, the company said it had assets and liabilities between $50 million and $100 million.”

item.title: South Korea Investigates Possible Use of A.I. in Hackings on Its Banks
item.description: New York Times: “South ⁠Korean officials are investigating whether artificial intelligence agents were involved in recent hacking incidents against banks in the country. President Lee Jae Myung said on Tuesday that “signs have emerged” that A.I. models had been used in some of the cyberattacks, ‘causing considerable public concern and anxiety.'”

item.title: Italy regulator probes AI music startup Suno over terms of service
item.description: Reuters: “Italy’s antitrust authority said on Tuesday it had opened an investigation ​into AI music startup Suno, ‌saying some clauses in its terms of service may be unfair to consumers.”

item.title: What’s Dragging Down A.I. Efficiency? The ‘Verification Tax.’
item.description: New York Times: “In survey after survey, executives and their employees report unimpressive gains from A.I. tools. Researchers from the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, Stanford University, the Bank of England and the Autonomous Technological Institute of Mexico recently published a poll of nearly 6,000 senior business executives in which about 90 percent said the technology had no impact on either employment or productivity. That’s even though 69 percent reported that their firms actively used A.I.”

item.title: Leading Chinese mathematicians unite behind use of AI in research
item.description: South China Morning Post: “Leading China’s mathematicians joined forces in Beijing on Sunday to launch an alliance aimed at integrating artificial intelligence into mathematical research. The Yau Laboratory Alliance for Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence is being spearheaded by Fields medallist Shing-Tung Yau, who warned that China was lagging behind the United States in using AI to advance frontier science.”

item.title: Award-winning microscopy image disqualified over AI use
item.description: Nature: “The winning entry of the prestigious Small World in Motion microscopy competition has been disqualified after scientists raised concerns about its creation using artificial intelligence. On 9 October, Nikon Instruments, which runs the competition, said in a statement that the winning video did not comply with competition rules. AI-generated videos are not permitted, according to the competition website.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: About page
item.description: Came in over the transom: RareCactus.com. From the “This rare cactus encyclopedia exists to help more people get into slow growing plants and to preserve them for the next generation after us. Many of these species are endangered in habitat, and a few are already effectively extinct in the wild. Learning where they come from and how to care for them properly is part of keeping them around.”

item.title: Experience Revolutionary War Pensions Like Never Before with Our New & Improved Full-Text Search and Transcription Viewer!
item.description: Fold3: “Genealogy and military research just got a massive upgrade! We’ve unlocked 2.4 million pages of Revolutionary War Pension Files with a state-of-the-art, patent-pending Transcription Viewer. The Transcription Viewer is unlike anything you’ve ever seen and is designed to make reading historical manuscripts faster, clearer, and much less frustrating.”

item.title: Find Movies – by Location & Period!
item.description: Maps Mania: “If you have a keen interest in watching a movie set in a particular time and place, then TitleAtlas is the interactive map for you. For example, you could use TitleAtlas to search for films set in 19th-century New York (Gangs of New York, Little Women, etc), or to find movies set in London during the Swinging Sixties (The Krays, Quadrophenia, etc).”

item.title: Online Newspaper Archive’s Future May Be Safe
item.description: Manx News: “Last month, [Manx National Heritage] revealed the serviced would be ‘temporarily’ unavailable, from today (October 12). It was due to be switched off while other options were explored. That led to concerns about its long-term future. However, MNH at the weekend said the switch off may only be for parts of today as it tried out a short-term solution. It also thanked users for their outpouring of support when news of the archive’s uncertain future first broke.”

item.title: Let’s Encrypt cuts certificate lifetimes to 64 days starting February 2027
item.description: Ars Technica: “Prior to Let’s Encrypt’s launch in early 2016, certificates were often issued for as long as one to three years. The service started with 90-day certificates to force renewal automation that didn’t previously exist. Shorter certificate validity periods limited vulnerabilities from private key thefts and encouraged accelerated HTTPS adoption across the web…. Just as the initial rollout of Let’s Encrypt aimed to push users toward HTTPS, the shortened certificate windows are aimed at moving users to full ACME automation.”

item.title: Cartoon Network Gigaleak Hits Days After Skydance Merger: Teen Titans, Gumball, Adventure Time
item.description: Cosmic Book News: “A massive leak of Cartoon Network production files is spreading online, and fans are calling it the Classic CN Gigaleak. Reports put the trove at more than 200 GB of internal material from over 30 shows, including The Amazing World of Gumball, Adventure Time, The Looney Tunes Show, Regular Show, Teen Titans, The Powerpuff Girls, and more.”

item.title: Fridges in French supermarkets hit by cyber attack
item.description: BBC: “Hundreds of French supermarkets have been hit by a cyber attack that caused their fridges and freezers to heat up, spoiling fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.”

item.title: A smart coffee maker uploaded 1TB of data in 10 days, and nobody knows why
item.description: TechSpot: “An IT worker was recently shocked to discover that his parents’ Keurig coffee maker had uploaded more than a terabyte of data in just 10 days. While a bug is the likely cause, the episode highlights the growing risks of connecting more and more mundane devices to the internet.”

item.title: Opinion: The Census Bureau is shutting out local data experts
item.description: CT Mirror: “Right now, the U.S. Census Bureau is quietly rewriting the rules for how people will be counted in 2030. These rules will change 250 years of precedent and will disadvantage Connecticut. But instead of working with state leaders to get it right, federal officials have done something alarming: They have stopped talking to us altogether.”

item.title: Someone Posted an Instagram Selfie. Scientists Spotted a Giant New Species in the Background
item.description: Gizmodo: “In research out this week, scientists describe having found a new species of giant waterlily that was initially spotted in an Instagram post. That post eventually set the researchers out on a journey through Colombia, where they were able to confirm the plant’s existence at the last possible second. Unfortunately, though, the waterlily may already be critically endangered.”

item.title: Tents, night-vision goggles and bear tracking kits: America’s first nature library opens
item.description: The Guardian: “The library offers people in Colorado’s Adams county the opportunity to borrow books and equipment to help them to engage with the natural world – for free. While most of the 40,000 items in the library’s collection are books, members can also check out 850 nature-focused ‘try it’ kits – anything from birdwatching equipment, gardening tools and wildlife cameras to hiking gear, microscopes and hammocks.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: The Puzzle Republic
item.description: Spotted on Bluesky: “A network of free puzzle libraries around the world.​” Little Free Puzzle Libraries, in other words… Sadly the closest one to me is in Chapel Hill, which is a couple of counties away….

item.title: ASCII.rest
item.description: Found in my RSS feeds: “217 animated ascii pieces for web pages: 15 full-colour scenes like the one above, loaders, charts, type, 29 language logos, 21 company logos and 23 Linux distros in colour or one ink, and 3D shapes, physics and creatures. Each is a small, typed TypeScript module with no dependencies, for React, Next.js, Astro, or a plain HTML page, and free to use and change under the MIT license.”

item.title: Russia’s Yandex says data centre in Vladimir area shut down after drone attack
item.description: Reuters: “Russian technology and AI company Yandex said on Sunday ​that its infrastructure had been ‌damaged in a drone attack, resulting in the complete shutdown of its data ​centre in the Vladimir region. No ​one was injured in the attack, ⁠but some of Yandex’s services ​are currently unavailable to users, the ​company said.”

item.title: Google Discover To Undergo Dramatic Changes
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “A new job posting for a Principal UX Lead for Discover, appears to indicate that Google is planning a substantial transformation of Discover, their recommendation engine for articles. The posting strongly suggests that Google plans to overhaul Discover into an AI-powered experience to become more deeply personalized.”

item.title: Google brings Health Guardian to the Fitbit Air and Edge, and expands automatic activity tracking
item.description: Engadget: “With the new Health Guardian features, Fitbit Air and Fitbit Edge users will receive a monthly summary in the Health app of their blood pressure and insulin resistance trends. The in-app Health Coach will provide lifestyle and wellness recommendations based on these readings, and insights to help you talk to your doctor about any concerns.”

item.title: Teenage figure skaters increasingly targeted by social media abuse as campaign launches
item.description: Associated Press: “Teenage figure skaters as young as 13 are being increasingly targeted by abusive comments on social media, Olympic gold medalist Evan Bates has warned. In a sport which has seen revived popularity since the 2026 Milan Cortina Winter Olympics, Bates said some users were creating ‘toxic environments’ around livestreamed events like Junior Grand Prix figure skating. That’s a key event for competitors aged 13 and older with dreams of becoming Olympians in the future.”

item.title: Canadian cyber executive charged in federal hacking case
item.description: Politico: “Edward Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on how to handle cyber extortion, is now charged with conspiracy to commit that very crime by threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, court records show. A court complaint detailing the allegations against Dubrovsky remains under seal.”

item.title: Using AI for just 10 minutes erodes your ability to persist at hard things
item.description: UC Berkeley: “Researchers recently found that spending just 10 minutes relying on an AI tool significantly impairs the user’s ability to focus and persist with difficult tasks. A preliminary draft made waves earlier this year, and the team presented the updated, peer-reviewed paper this week at the Conference on Language Modeling.”

item.title: PBS adds France 24 English to digital streaming lineup
item.description: TheDesk: “PBS has reached a distribution agreement with international news broadcaster France 24 that will allow its member stations to offer a livestream of France 24 English through PBS digital platforms in the United States.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: AI model submitted false tip about unsolved murder, Philadelphia police say
item.description: 6ABC: “An Anthropic A.I. model submitted a false tip about an unsolved murder through a publicly accessible web form, Philadelphia police said Friday. The tip was sent through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com back on July 18, but was flagged as spam and never acted upon.”

item.title: Anthropic can’t reliably control its AI agents. It’s cutting off its internal evals from the live internet instead
item.description: TechCrunch: “Anthropic said its models exploited websites on the internet, including some run by U.S. government agencies, and it will turn off live internet access for all of its internal evaluations until the frontier lab is sure it can monitor and control its AI agents.”

item.title: Google data center project in Chesterfield racks up seven environmental violations from state
item.description: WRIC: “The Project Peanut data center site — the first of three planned by Google in Chesterfield — has racked up seven violations over the course of about eight months, according to a letter sent to Google on Sept. 29 from the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ). The letter alleges that DEQ Virginia Water Protection Staff received emails about unauthorized filling of surface waters outside of the Project Peanut site on several different occasions from December 2025 to August 2026. DEQ said that between January and August, staff conducted five inspections.”

item.title: How Local Debates Over Data Centers Leak into Water Scarcity Concerns
item.description: University of Georgia: “Although people benefit from the services provided by utilities and artificial intelligence, local communities share finite water resources with energy generating infrastructure. According to a report by Ceres, power plants and data centers built in drought-prone areas directly compete with local communities, agriculture and ecosystems with local water resources. The Environmental Protection Division of Georgia requires a water permit if a facility uses more than 100,000 gallons of water per day from local surface water sources, which many large data centers and power plants exceed dramatically.”

item.title: Inside Mark Zuckerberg’s Decision to Pull the Trigger on Meta’s A.I. Agent
item.description: New York Times: “A 14-person start-up called Instinct had created an A.I. agent, which are bots that can operate apps and software on behalf of users, and it was taking off. Meta was developing a similar product called Muse, but had delayed releasing it over safety concerns. Fearful of losing a competitive edge, Mr. Zuckerberg said Muse was ready to launch despite the risks, according to three people with knowledge of the meeting, who were not authorized to speak publicly on confidential matters.”

item.title: Condé Nast, Hearst among 300 publishers pressuring Congress to ban bot scraping
item.description: Mashable: “Executives from iconic publications like Esquire, Cosmopolitan, Vogue, and Vanity Fair are descending on Washington to lobby for another AI regulation bill, this time tackling the threat AI poses to their bottom lines and longevity.”

item.title: Fake Caroline
item.description: Columbia Journalism Review: “Fake Caroline’s ruse unraveled over the summer as editors at multiple science magazines, who had all received pitches from the impostor, separately notified Williams about suspicious emails, prompting her to post a frantic warning, with screenshots of the impostor’s messages, on LinkedIn: ‘EDITORS: THIS IS NOT ME!!!’ By mid-September, an editor at Science saw Williams’s pleas and connected the dots.”

item.title: AI startup touts new possibilities for video creators, but concerns remain
item.description: PBS Newshour: “As AI continues to reshape arts and entertainment, it’s also creating a new type of producers and content providers. A Silicon Valley start-up founded by a YouTube co-founder could change video storytelling as dramatically as he changed video distribution. Special correspondent Mike Cerre reports for our arts & culture series, CANVAS.”

item.title: OpenAI defends decision to fire researchers: ‘These decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out’
item.description: CNBC: “OpenAI on Friday defended its decision to fire three safety researchers, saying they had committed a ‘significant breach of trust.’ The AI lab said in a post on X that its decision to part ways with Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni, was not about the fact that they had raised safety concerns.”

item.title: Swedish ball-bearing ad revives Greta Garbo with US, Chinese AI
item.description: Reuters: “‘Are we rolling?’ the AI likeness of Hollywood ​1930s movie star Greta Garbo lilts, in an unlikely advert for Swedish ball-bearings maker SKF. The ‌advert has sparked debate, praise and ridicule, but underscores how sophisticated AI is increasingly encroaching on media from script-writing to animation.”

item.title: We Might Be Cooked, As These Vibe-Coded Web Browser Ports Of Halo, The Simpsons: Hit And Run, And GTA: Vice City Seem To Work Perfectly
item.description: Kotaku: “In the past couple of weeks, hundreds of vibe-coded, AI-decompiled emulators and games have appeared out of thin air. Why? Because Claude’s latest update, Claude Opus 5.5, is extremely good at decompiling.”

item.title: Sentence tossed in Arizona case where deceased victim was depicted speaking in AI-generated video
item.description: Associated Press: “An Arizona man’s 10-year manslaughter sentence has been tossed in a case where a video generated by artificial intelligence portrayed the deceased victim addressing a judge before the punishment was imposed…. The court found the video crossed the line, saying it didn’t reflect actual events and presented statements made in the footage as coming directly from the victim.”

item.title: YouTubers’ data scraping suit against ByteDance lives on
item.description: Courthouse News Service: “A federal judge ruled Friday YouTubers have standing in a suit accusing tech giant ByteDance of data mining their videos to train artificial intelligence models U.S. District Judge Jacqueline Scott Corley ruled that Ted Entertainment and Matt Fisher properly claimed at this stage that they’ve suffered what she called a pocketbook injury.”

item.title: Hojun Son Receives SUNY AI Research Grant to Unlock Stony Brook University’s The Statesman Archive!
item.description: Stony Brook University: “Using Stony Brook University’s The Statesman and a corpus of more than 50,000 newspaper manuscripts, Hojun [Sun] will investigate how the diverse content in historical newspapers can be integrated, represented and explored through multimodal AI approaches. His work aims to enhance understanding of historical content while improving search, discovery and access to these valuable archival resources.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Dibrugarh University digitises 53,275 pages of rare Sanchipat manuscripts
item.description: Assam Tribune: “Marking the birth centenary of noted Assamese poet Nabakanta Barua, Dibrugarh University on October 6 launched what is described as the country’s largest online archive of rare Sanchipat manuscripts, making thousands of pages of invaluable literary and cultural heritage freely accessible to people across the globe.”

item.title: 525 rare manuscripts from scholar İsmail Erünsal made available online
item.description: Hurriyet Daily News: “A collection of 525 rare works donated by Ottoman book and library history scholar İsmail Erünsal to Istanbul’s Süleymaniye Manuscript Library has been digitized and opened to public access worldwide. The collection, assembled by Erünsal over decades through his personal efforts, includes unique copies, rare works and manuscripts written in the authors’ own handwriting.”

item.title: Free Online Archive Of PS1 & N64 3D Models & Game Assets
item.description: 80 LV: “Retro gaming fans and game developers looking to learn from classic titles should check out Pardall Games, a solo project by Alfred Baudisch. Essentially, it’s an interactive digital museum and archive of assets from PlayStation, Nintendo 64, and Sega Saturn games.”

item.title: Trump Vowed to Wall Off TikTok From China. Did He?
item.description: Politico: “Employees at the new company, officially named TikTok USDS Joint Venture, still work regularly with the global TikTok organization, according to current and former employees, who were granted anonymity to speak candidly, and internal communications reviewed by POLITICO Magazine. That includes coordinating over new features, sharing information about dangerous trends on the app and collaborating over policies. U.S. employees also still use an internal chat system called Lark, which was built by TikTok’s former Beijing-based parent company, ByteDance, to communicate and share information with both their U.S. and global counterparts.”

item.title: Ukraine hits second major tech site, expanding range of targets inside Russia
item.description: Reuters: “Ukraine struck and partly disabled a major data ​centre operated by Russian technology company Yandex on Friday in the second such action in successive days, widening the scope of its attacks inside Russia after ‌Moscow hit data hubs in Ukraine.”

item.title: ‘We’ve been here in Bury for over 20 years, then Google suddenly said we don’t exist’
item.description: Manchester Evening News: “Jay, who runs The PC Guy, said he discovered that his Google Business Profile had been disabled after someone suggested to Google that his long-established business had permanently closed. The computer specialist, who has been working in the industry for more than 20 years and opened his Bury office in 2013, said the removal had already started to affect the number of calls coming into the business.”

item.title: Chicago Public Media begins rollout of Chicago.com, in exclusive partnership with RoundTable
item.description: Evanston RoundTable: “Chicago Public Media (CPM) has started its rollout of Chicago.com, a neighbor-focused social media platform launching with five pilot communities… The five pilot communities are Evanston, Avondale, Bronzeville, Edgewater/Andersonville and South Shore. The first phase started Wednesday in Avondale. The Evanston community will officially launch Monday, Oct. 12.”

item.title: Owner of Empire cybercrime market gets 40 years in prison
item.description: Bleeping Computer: “The co-creator of Empire Market, one of the largest dark web marketplaces before its shutdown, has been sentenced to 40 years in prison for facilitating $430 million in illegal transactions from 2018 to 2020.”

item.title: Ohio political blogger found guilty in explicit Shrek meme trial
item.description: Ohio Capital Journal: “After just thirty minutes, eight Lake County jurors decided D.J. Byrnes was guilty of telecommunications harassment against state Sen. Jerry Cirino (R-Kirtland), after he sent him two taunting messages and a meme of Shrek holding his genitals.”

item.title: Greece and US Renew Cultural Heritage Protection Agreement
item.description: Greek City Times: “Greece and the United States have renewed an agreement restricting the import of certain categories of Greek archaeological and ethnological material into the US, extending the measures for another five years through 2031.”

item.title: Climbers scale St. Louis trees during international tree climbing competition
item.description: Associated Press: “Nearly 100 arborists clad in helmets and rope harnesses scaled pine, sweetgum and oak trees in a St. Louis park Friday during the International Tree Climbing Championship. This year marks the competition’s 50th anniversary, where contestants from 22 countries are showcasing their climbing finesse over three days.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: About
item.description: Found in my RSS feeds: Map Animator. From the page: “Map Animator makes animated route maps for travel and adventure videos, right in your browser. It’s made for people who film their trips: motorcycle tours, cycling, hiking, road trips and sailing. Draw the route or use your GPX recording, give it a look, and get a video clip that shows where you went. Everything happens on your own computer. Your projects are stored in your browser and your videos are made in your browser, so nothing about your trips is sent to us.”

item.title: Ministry For Heritage Launches New Educational History Video Series
item.description: Government of Gibraltar: “The videos will cover a broad range of subjects spanning Gibraltar’s history, archaeology, culture, language, people and heritage. They will draw upon the extensive body of work already undertaken by the Ministry for Heritage and will complement the information already available through interpretation panels, heritage trails, educational resources and the Ministry’s website. The aim is to make Gibraltar’s history more accessible, engaging and understandable, particularly for younger audiences who increasingly consume educational content through digital platforms.”

item.title: EBSCO Information Services Launches Urban Studies Source Database for Urban Research
item.description: PR Newswire: (PRESS RELEASE). “EBSCO Information Services (EBSCO) has launched Urban Studies Source, a new full-text research database focused on cities, urban communities, and the forces shaping them. Designed to support interdisciplinary teaching and research, the multidisciplinary resource provides international perspectives on the historical, social, economic, environmental and physical dimensions of urban development.”

item.title: Google Opens Search Profiles In India & Canada, Brazil Next
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “Google is opening Search profiles to creators and publishers in India and Canada. Until today, the profiles were only open in the U.S., where they launched in June. Robby Stein, VP of Product for Google Search, announced the expansion on X. Search profiles are claimable pages that pull a source’s articles and social posts together.”

item.title: Twitch has streaming deals in its new Shopping category
item.description: Tubefilter: “Live streams have become the new QVC programs, and Twitch is hopping onto the bandwagon. The Amazon-owned platform is linking up with its parent company to populate a new Shopping category that showcases streamers who are selling products to their viewers.”

item.title: Florida asks court to force Meta to change Facebook, Instagram for teens
item.description: Reuters: “Florida ​asked a state judge on Wednesday to order changes to Instagram and Facebook to better ‌protect young users, pressing ahead with a lawsuit accusing parent Meta Platforms of harming teens after most states resolved similar claims through a sweeping settlement.”

item.title: Norway wants to temporarily ban smart glasses in parks, beaches, and schools
item.description: TechSpot: “Norwegian authorities are preparing a temporary ban on AI-enhanced smart glasses, giving experts time to draft a new law that restricts potential abuse of the latest wearables. The government announced the plan on Monday, saying smart glasses will become an unwelcome guest in certain public places, at least for the time being.”

item.title: Data Science professor awarded grant to support partnership with Internet Archive and preserve digital history
item.description: William & Mary: “To help fight the loss of digital media, Dr. Alexander Nwala is leading a collaborative research project, CiteCast, to preserve web resources referenced in U.S. television news. Backed by a new $750,000 grant from the Institute of Museum and Library Services, Nwala, in collaboration with Old Dominion University and the Internet Archive, will develop AI models that automatically identify, archive and catalog these referenced web pages in a publicly accessible database, ensuring they remain available to researchers, journalists and future generations.”

item.title: Leave a paper trail or get lost in history
item.description: Daily Mississippian: “The answer is not to abandon digital archives, as they have allowed historical information to be more accessible for public viewing. We should strive to preserve and create more physical media. Physical newspapers, photographs, letters, records and other forms of physical media provide another way for future generations to understand us. Our generation has more of everyday life documented than any generation before us, but documentation does not mean preservation.”

item.title: How a Calvert Museum Idea Became Maryland’s State Shark
item.description: Southern Maryland Chronicle: “The idea started as a casual question between two people at the Calvert Marine Museum: why not make megalodon the state shark? As of Oct. 1, it is. Maryland’s official state shark is Otodus megalodon, the extinct giant known mostly from its fossil teeth, and the Calvert Marine Museum says Maryland is the first state in the nation to recognize an official state shark.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Massachusetts Doesn’t Have A Public Database Of Ethics Disclosures, So He Made One
item.description: BINJ News: “For his latest project, StateReference Ethics, Story dragged another set of hard-to-get records into public view. Per his description, it’s a ‘searchable database of ethics disclosures filed by Massachusetts officials detailing their investments, potential conflicts of interest, and more.’ We’re just getting started entering search terms like ‘Palantir’ and ‘Axon’ into the dashboard, and discovering innumerable leads for future coverage of our electeds and the interests which entertain them.”

item.title: Before You Take That Job or Stay Put, New Data Reveals if Women Actually Get Promoted There
item.description: PR Newswire: (PRESS RELEASE). “Type nearly any major U.S. employer’s name into a free public site recently launched by data scientists and funded by the Women Leaders Association, and see its Glass Ceiling Score: a simple measure of whether women there rise into management and executive jobs at the same rate as men, calculated from the company’s actual workforce numbers — not its recruiting brochure.”

item.title: Emory Launches Interactive Map Projecting Health, Economic Costs of Declining Vaccine Coverage
item.description: Emory University: “VaxImpactMap uses epidemiological models and state-level data to project the additional disease cases, hospitalizations, deaths, missed workdays, and health care costs that would occur at different levels of declining vaccination coverage.”

item.title: North Korea renames cultural agency to erase ‘national’ identity with South
item.description: NK News: “The agency formerly known as the Bureau for the Protection of National Cultural Heritage (민족유산보호국) is now know as the Bureau for the Protection of Historical Heritage (력사유산보호국), according to a state-run Korean Central News Agency report on Sunday.”

item.title: Journalist groups urge X to reject broad account-blocking requests in Turkey
item.description: Reuters: “Journalism groups called on social media platform X on Tuesday not to accept requests by ​the authorities to restrict access to accounts ‌held by journalists and media outlets in Turkey without a clear and independently reviewable judicial decision.”

item.title: Fitness influencer posts her Berlin Marathon victory. Then she is caught on a bicycle at the 38km mark: ‘This was extremely dishonest’
item.description: The Mary Sue: “Chinese fitness influencer Abeeeer, who has around 530,000 social media followers, celebrated completing the September 27 Berlin Marathon in 4:53:46. Later, photos circulated showing her riding on the back of a bicycle near the 38-kilometer mark, according to Dexerto.”

item.title: Russia’s internet giant Yandex halts operations at major data center after drone attack
item.description: CNBC: “Russian internet giant Yandex suspended operations at one of its key data centers on Thursday after a drone strike as Ukraine continues to target the country’s infrastructure.”

item.title: 713 deepfakes of political leaders taken offline
item.description: New Straits Times: “A total of 713 image-manipulation and deepfake content involving political party leaders have been taken down between Jan 1, 2025 and Sept 15 this year. The Communications Ministry said the content was taken down following complaints, breaches of service providers’ community guidelines and violations of local laws.”

item.title: Exclusive: Archaeology megafirm abruptly shuts down
item.description: Science: “Chronicle Heritage, which was backed by venture capitalists and formed through the merger of several smaller firms, was a major player in the for-profit cultural heritage industry. It had more than 20 offices and an estimated annual revenue of $100 million. Such firms are often contracted to conduct legally required archaeological surveys and other reviews prior to major development projects. They have been a major source of archaeological data, and some observers estimate they conducted up to 90% of the archaeological research performed in the U.S. each year.”

item.title: How ‘Digital Oblivion’ Is Helping Russia Rewrite the Past
item.description: Moscow Times: “The disappearance of independent journalism, firsthand accounts and historical archives from the internet is helping Russia and other authoritarian states rewrite history and shape collective memory, researchers warn. From altered reporting on the Beslan school siege to vanishing articles documenting anti-government protests, the loss of online records — a process that researchers call ‘digital oblivion’ — is contributing to public ‘amnesia’ about key events that autocrats find unhelpful.”

item.title: New method turns urban and industrial noise into a tool for monitoring the subsurface
item.description: GEO3BCN: “Researchers from Geosciences Barcelona (GEO3BCN), part of the Spanish National Research Council (CSIC), has developed a pioneering method that uses noise generated by human activity to monitor the subsurface continuously and non-invasively. The technique, called REFTION, was tested with data from a network of seismic stations installed at the Riotinto mine in Huelva, an especially complex environment because of the many sources of industrial noise.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Solo teen hiker hoisted from mountain cliff after using AI to plan route, North Shore Rescue says
item.description: North Shore News: “The hiker started on Grouse Mountain around 8 a.m., aiming to do a route that went up Crown Mountain, said search manager Paul Markey. AI had planned a route that ascended Crown Mountain by a gully. But when the hiker was following the trail, it actually led him to a rock-climbing route with steep terrain. The teen got stuck at the base of a cliff.”

item.title: Meta Is Refusing to Remove AI-Generated Facebook Videos of Graphic Child Abuse, Including a Baby Roasting in an Oven
item.description: Futurism: “Last month, we reported that Facebook was hosting enormous numbers of graphic AI-generated videos of physical child abuse that showed kids being beaten, burned, dragged by their hair, locked in cages, and more. In response to our questions, Facebook’s parent company Meta alternately dragged its feet, rationalized about why the videos were acceptable, and issued hard-to-parse statements that dodged any accountability or meaningful commitment to fighting the phenomenon.”

item.title: Most Utahns oppose building more data centers. Here’s what they want done about them.
item.description: Salt Lake Tribune: “As the number of planned data center projects seemingly explodes across Utah, most residents aren’t happy with how their elected leaders have handled them, according to a new survey. A vast majority of Utahns – 86% – also don’t feel the cost of data centers, including their water and energy demands, outweigh their touted economic benefits, according to results from Utah State University’s Community and Natural Resources Institute’s survey. And nearly 76% of residents oppose or strongly oppose building more data centers in Utah.”

item.title: Google ordered to halt work on two data centers in ‘Texas of Europe’
item.description: CNBC: “Finnish Licensing and Supervision Agency (LVV) on Tuesday issued a notice to Google subsidiary, Tuike Finland Oy, to suspend building work for data center projects planned for Muhos and Kajaani until the environmental impact assessments have been completed.”

item.title: Coalition of AI giants, labor unions proposes uniform guardrails for Indiana data centers
item.description: Mirror Indy: “A national coalition of AI companies, labor unions and investors is launching a campaign in Indiana calling for tighter guardrails on new data centers while pushing back against local moratoriums. The American Infrastructure Alliance (AIA), a multi-million-dollar cohort of 20 organizations, began in September working with local and state officials to implement standards around data center developments.”

item.title: German search engine ditches Mistral, bets on Chinese open-source AI
item.description: Politico: “A Berlin-based search engine used by government services is dropping its French AI partner, Mistral, in favor of open-source models, including those from China, its CEO told POLITICO.”

item.title: Particularly Weak-Minded Americans Are Asking ChatGPT Which Candidate to Vote For, Which Sounds a Bit Like AI Is Just Voting Now Via Meat Proxies
item.description: Futurism: “In a new piece, NPR spoke to several voters who use the OpenAI chatbot to research candidates and get a rundown on their voting records. Some are asking the AI to create spreadsheets on different races or to verify or debunk viral claims. One even used AI to create an entire website for retrieving voting info. Experts are aghast, noting that AI models tend to be sycophantic and aren’t as impartial as they seem.”

item.title: Italy’s Meloni follows pop stars in seeking to trademark her voice to combat AI deepfakes
item.description: Associated Press: “Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni has applied to trademark her voice with the European Union’s Intellectual Property Office, seeking to protect herself against AI-generated deepfakes. The application filed with the EU agency includes a four-second audio recording of Meloni repeating the phrase, in Italian, ‘Io sono Giorgia Meloni’ (“I am Giorgia Meloni”), according to the EU office’s records on Monday.”

item.title: OpenAI Decides ChatGPT Would Be Better With More Sponsored Results
item.description: Gizmodo: “Hey! You got ads in my AI responses! On Monday, OpenAI announced that it plans to start expanding the types of advertisements that appear in ChatGPT alongside the model’s outputs.”

item.title: Visual investigation: Online resellers using AI to pretend to be mom-and-pop stores
item.description: ABC News: “Scores of online companies are increasingly turning to generative AI technology to deceive consumers, falsely portraying themselves as struggling small businesses to charge a premium for lower quality products, an ABC News visual investigation found. ABC News has identified dozens of similar online retailers — selling everything from clothing to jewelry to lamps — that used AI images and videos to portray themselves as down-on-their-luck craftsmen or small business owners in need of support.”

item.title: AI Music Streaming Fraudster Sentenced to 1.5 Years in Prison for $8M Royalties Scam
item.description: Billboard: “Michael Smith, 54, pleaded guilty in March to using AI to generate thousands of songs and then streaming them billions of times with bots, generating more than $8 million in royalties. His was the first criminal conviction over a tricky problem that’s plagued the music industry for years.”

item.title: California issues investigative subpoena to OpenAI over rogue agents’ hacking
item.description: The Guardian: “California’s attorney general has issued an investigative subpoena to OpenAI, starting an investigation into the startup ⁠as ​part of a broader inquiry into potential cybersecurity vulnerabilities and incidents related ⁠to its AI models, his office said on Thursday.”

item.title: OpenAI says teens use ChatGPT for under 15 minutes a day as worries over risks grow
item.description: Reuters: “Teens spend under 15 minutes a day on average on ChatGPT, while less than 2% of them interact with the chatbot for over three straight hours, OpenAI ​said, as technology companies face scrutiny over the risks AI chatbots pose to children. Sam Altman’s ‌AI company released the figures in its first report on teen use on Wednesday as rapid adoption of AI platforms raises concerns about their impact on adolescent mental health and developmental safety.” With the caveat that these numbers come from OpenAI.

item.title: Anthropic Claude subscription plan provides more value than OpenAI’s, study says
item.description: The Register: “Following changes to OpenAI’s $200 per month subscription plan that effectively halved its value, SemiAnalysis looked at the various subscription plans offered by AI companies, because that’s still the main way that individuals and small businesses buy AI services.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: Google Launches New Website to Detect AI Fakes, But Don’t Assume It’s Perfect
item.description: Gizmodo: “The image above isn’t real. Sure, Ken Paxton and Donald Trump are political allies, and Trump starred in a McDonald’s commercial featuring Grimace back in 2002, so it’s entirely plausible that they all appeared on a golf course together. But it’s fake. And one way to check that is with a new portal from Google…. There’s one big catch: It can only detect fake images made with tools from Google, OpenAI, Nvidia, and Kakao.”

item.title: Rare ‘fragile’ recordings saved before they disappear
item.description: BBC: “Hundreds of recordings capturing the voices, accents and memories of people across the South West are being rescued before fragile tapes deteriorate beyond repair. Archivists say some are at risk of being lost forever as ageing cassette and reel-to-reel tapes begin to break down. The Sounds of the South West project is digitising them, preserving everything from Cornish dialect and sea shanties to memories of salmon fishing on the River Severn.”

item.title: George Eastman Museum workers vote to unionize
item.description: Rochester Beacon: “Workers at the George Eastman Museum voted 41-16 to unionize with Workers United, according to the organizing group, George Eastman Museum Workers United. The National Labor Relations Board election was held Friday, Oct. 2, and the group announced the result Sunday.”

item.title: Meet The Social Media Influencers Spreading Mayor Brandon Johnson’s Message
item.description: Block Club Chicago: “A squad of like-minded progressive content creators caught the attention of many this September when an Instagram reel of several creators dancing with Mayor Brandon Johnson went viral. The caption announced he was officially running for reelection. Later that evening, Johnson formally addressed a crowd of supporters to announce he was officially in the race as the incumbent. At that announcement were several content creators seen in that viral video.”

item.title: British man stranded in forest rescued by police, praises Vietnam’s kindness
item.description: VN Express: “[Barry] Mattacott, who works as a marketing specialist in Vietnam, was riding a Kawasaki W650 around noon on Oct. 3 when, following directions from Google Maps, he turned onto a dirt road through the mountains and forest in Dang Thuy Tram Commune, Quang Ngai Province. The road became increasingly difficult, with steep sections, rough rocks and mud. In some places, the motorcycle sank halfway into the mud. Eventually, the bike suffered a flat tire on a rocky slope.”

item.title: Denver woman sues Flock, police after being accused of a crime she didn’t commit
item.description: Denver Post: “When Columbine Valley police Sgt. Jamie Milliman knocked on Chrisanna Elser’s door in southwest Denver’s Fort Logan neighborhood on Sept. 27, 2025, he said he was certain he had caught a thief. Milliman had never met Elser and had never spoken to her, but used Flock cameras to ‘digitally stalk’ the woman and erroneously connect her to a stolen package in Bow Mar, according to the lawsuit filed Monday in U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado.”

item.title: How the TikTok algorithm changed political campaigning in 2024
item.description: PsyPost: “A recent study shows that political candidates on TikTok garner more views and interactions when they use short, highly emotional, and performance-based videos rather than detailed policy discussions. The research reveals how the structural design of the app encourages political messaging that prioritizes quick entertainment and visual spectacle over traditional campaigning. The findings were published in the Journal of Political Marketing.”

item.title: 96-year-old Maine woman is done watching weather for NOAA
item.description: Bangor Daily News: “Every Wednesday at 8 a.m. on the dot, Arlene Cole has called The Lincoln County News to send in the weather report. Now at 96, Cole has retired. Her last report was in the Thursday edition of the paper. After spending more than 60 years monitoring and logging temperatures, rain, snow and more, she said it was time to stop before the weather gets too harsh in the winter.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Queer Up North Digital Archive launches
item.description: About Manchester: “An extraordinary new digital archive documenting the history of Queer Up North (1992-2002) has launched The archive reveals stories about the people, performances, club nights, cabaret, comedy and art that helped to shape queer culture in 90s Manchester, bringing together objects from the festival’s colourful history and making them collectively available to the public for the first time – freely and online.”

item.title: WordPress 7.1.3 Fixes 7 Vulnerabilities And 1 Critical Flaw
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “WordPress announced a security release to address seven security vulnerabilities plus four bug fixes. This security release, Version 7.1.3, addresses a stored XSS, denial-of-service DoS and five other vulnerabilities of undisclosed severity level. WordPress recommends updating sites immediately.”

item.title: One Tech Tip: Lake America backlash fuels interest in Google Maps alternatives
item.description: Associated Press: “After President Donald Trump ordered a new name for Lake Ontario, the two U.S. tech giants quickly fell in line, relabeling the body of water on their digital maps. The move sparked a backlash among some users, already unhappy with the companies’ decisions to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America on their maps following a previous Trump edict.”

item.title: I stopped handing my real email to random websites, here’s what I use instead
item.description: MakeUseOf: “I used to hand over the same address almost everywhere and deal with the resulting newsletters, promotions, and mystery mailing lists later. Now I treat my real email more like my phone number and decide how permanent an address should be before giving it away. A website I need for ten minutes gets treated very differently from an account I may still be logging into three years from now.”

item.title: ICANN reveals bids for new top-level domains
item.description: The Register: “For years, only ICANN could create and operate GTLDs. The governance body changed that policy and in 2012 allowed over 1,200 new GTLDs. The organization decided to repeat the process this year and on Wednesday announced it received 1,615 applications. A process is now under way to confirm those applications are viable.”

item.title: Hollywood tears into Big Tech
item.description: Politico: “Hollywood is turning on Big Tech. In a run of films arriving this fall, the industry casts Mark Zuckerberg, Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Elizabeth Holmes as venal, feckless, cowardly, cruel or worse — villains in a new, on-screen front in the backlash over Silicon Valley’s power. And the pile-on may not end there.”

item.title: Thousands of European wind and solar power systems exposed online, Dutch researchers say
item.description: Reuters: “Thousands of administrative systems at wind and solar power parks in Europe are exposed to the ‌internet, potentially giving attackers access to interfaces that can stop turbines and raising the risk of sabotage, Dutch researchers warned on Tuesday. The exposed systems included administrative and login interfaces as well as operational interfaces showing data and controls.”

item.title: Lexington couple questions Flock cameras after lead mismatches their car in road-rage case
item.description: Lex18: “A Lexington couple is questioning the city’s use of Flock cameras after police arrived at their home with guns drawn early Saturday morning while investigating a violent road-rage incident. Will Penn and Robin Pen say multiple officers surrounded their property at 3:56 a.m. Saturday. Ring doorbell footage shows police vehicles pulling up, and by 4:08 a.m., spotlights were shining on the home as officers surrounded it.”

item.title: Poland’s antitrust regulator accuses Google of unfair market practices
item.description: Engadget: “A Polish regulator said that Google isn’t playing by the rules when the tech giant displays articles from local media publishers in Google Search, Google News and Google Discover. Poland’s Office of Competition and Consumer Protection, abbreviated as UOKiK, said that Google leaned on its dominant market position and failed to provide necessary data when negotiating compensation with the country’s news publishers.”

item.title: Focus on social media engagement – not just screen time – essential to help protect mental health
item.description: University of Exeter: “The research indicates that associations between social media use and depressive and anxiety symptoms depend not only on how frequently or how long individuals engage, but also on the cognitive, emotional, and behavioural quality of that engagement.”

item.title: Mapping the past and preserving the future
item.description: Northern Arizona University: “With a grant from Western National Parks, a team from the Department of Anthropology and NAU’s Radiant Center for Remote Sensing has partnered with the National Park Service (NPS) on the architectural documentation and digital mapping of Wukoki Pueblo, a site 30 miles north of Flagstaff within Wupatki National Monument.”

item.title: New framework aims to make digital evidence credible for medical device regulation
item.description: University of Manchester: “University of Manchester-led researchers have unveiled a roadmap for making computer-generated evidence trustworthy enough to help regulators decide whether medical devices are safe and effective, alongside laboratory and clinical evidence.” Good morning, Internet…
